newsitem.title: USA: Cardinals urge Clinton to ban abortion procedure.
newsitem.headline: Cardinals urge Clinton to ban abortion procedure.

text.p: U.S. Roman Catholic cardinals read an open letter to President Bill Clinton on Sunday urging him to sign a measure that would ban the so-called partial birth abortion procedure.

"Mr. President, you are in a unique position to ensure respect for all human rights, including the right to life which is denied to infants who are brutally killed in partial birth abortion," according to the letter signed by the seven U.S. cardinals.
"We urge you to ask Congress to pass a bill banning partial birth abortions, and let it be known that you will sign it into law," the letter continued.
Clinton, at a press conference on Friday, said any law on the contentious procedure should make sure that it is available to the few women who truly need it.

"I think you could make a very compelling case that for the small number of people I'm trying to protect this is the biggest issue in their entire lives and that for them my position is the pro-life position," Clinton told reporters.

"And I believe that it would be a mistake for us to pass this bill one more time without taking care of those folks," he added two days after a new bill banning the procedure was introduced in the House of Representatives.

Clinton has said he would be able to sign a bill that allowed the procedure to be performed to save the life or health of the woman. The current bill, like last year's, provides only for cases where the woman's life is at stake.

The issue has sparked heated debate since a ban was first introduced in Congress in 1995. The procedure involves the partial extraction of the foetus feet-first, the subsequent suctioning out of the brain and removal of the foetus.

The latest flareup began last week when Ron Fitzsimmons, executive director of the National Coalition of Abortion Providers, said he "lied through my teeth" when he defended this kind of late-term abortion.
Instead of the 500 or so a year cited by abortion rights advocates, he said as many as 5,000 might be performed, many on women in earlier stages of non-crisis pregnancies.
The House is expected to take up the measure before Easter.
